Pleasure? I... I don't even know if I'd use that word, or if I even remember what that really feels like, to be honest with you. It's hard to say. I mean, I guess I used to. I used to love the smell of the sawdust, you know? When you first cut into a fresh piece of cherry wood or mahogany... there's this sweet, almost earthy smell that just fills the whole shop. It gets in your clothes, your hair. My wife used to say I smelled like a forest when I came in for dinner. And I used to spend hours, just hours, sanding down the edges of a cabinet door, making sure the joints were perfectly flush. I only do dovetail joints, none of that cheap factory-made stuff with the staples and the glue. I'd run my bare hand over the final finish and just feel... proud, I guess? 

But now... I don't know. I'm not sure I feel anything at all when I'm out there. I've got this half-finished oak vanity sitting right in the middle of my workspace right now. It's been taking up space for three weeks. The client keeps calling, leaving voicemails, and my wife keeps telling me I need to go out there and finish it because the bank is breathing down our necks, and I know she's right. I know it. But I just... I go out there, I pick up the orbital sander, and I just stare at it. I don't feel any spark, I don't feel any pride. I'm not sure I feel anything except just this heavy, exhausting weight I told you about. So, pleasure? I really couldn't tell you. I haven't noticed feeling good about a piece of furniture in... gosh, years, maybe. It's just a block of dead wood to me now. Just another thing I have to do and can't bring myself to care about.

I wear these heavy Carhartt work pants—the double-front ones, you know, because I'm always kneeling on the concrete floor—and they've got a pretty rigid waistband. Sleep? No... no, sleep isn't really an issue for me. I don't have any trouble with that. 

I mean, by the time I finally drag myself in from the shop, I'm just dead on my feet. I usually lock up the bays around nine, maybe nine-thirty. Energy? No. God, no. I don't have energy for anything anymore. It's... it's like my tank is just permanently on empty, you know? 

I mean, I just told you I sleep like a rock, right? Seven, eight hours of solid sleep on that firm cherry wood bed I built. You'd think I'd wake up refreshed, ready to tackle the day, but I don't. I wake up and I'm already exhausted. It's a bone-deep kind of tired. By midmorning, usually around 10 or 10:30, after I've had my coffee and maybe run the table saw for a bit... my arms feel like lead. They feel like I've been hauling wet pressure-treated lumber all day long, just heavy and useless. And that's just from doing basic stuff. 

Even just pushing through the normal routine—measuring out cuts, standing at the chop saw, trying to focus on the grain of the wood so I don't mess up a piece of expensive white oak—it takes everything I have. And it's not just the physical work, either. It's the mental stuff. Returning phone calls to clients, trying to explain why a custom cabinet is delayed, or just looking at the invoices piled up on my desk... I can barely do it. I just feel completely wiped out. 

I remember a time, maybe five or six years ago, when I could work a twelve-hour day, frame out a whole kitchen, install the uppers, and still have enough energy to come home and grill steaks in the backyard with Sarah. I used to thrive on that kind of momentum. I liked the sweat, the ache in my muscles—it felt earned. But this? This isn't that good, honest kind of tired. This is just a heavy, dragging exhaustion that never goes away, no matter how much I sleep or how much coffee I drink. I just stand there in the shop, staring at the tools, feeling like I'm moving through molasses. So, no, I definitely don't have the energy to do what I need to do. I barely have the energy to stand upright most days.

Look forward to? No. No, not really. I... I can't really think of a single thing. 

It's funny, because I used to have a lot of things. I used to love going down to MacGregor's—that's the specialty lumber yard about forty minutes from here, out past the county line. I used to wake up early on a Saturday, grab a coffee, and just go walk the aisles. The smell of the rough-sawn walnut, the kiln-dried cherry... I just look at it and think about the weight of having to haul it into the truck, mill it down, joint it, plane it, sand it until my shoulders scream. 

Sarah even tried to get me to go to the lake last month, thought maybe getting the old aluminum boat out would help. We used to love fishing for bass in the early mornings. But... I spent two weeks dreading it. The packing, the driving, the sun beating down. I look at my week, or the weekend, or even just dinner tonight, and it's just a long stretch of gray. It's all just things I have to get through, one after the other, until I can finally go back to sleep. So, no. I'm not looking forward to anything. It all just feels like a burden now.

Enjoy? I... I don't really know if enjoy is the right word. I don't think I enjoy much of anything, like I was just saying. 

With Sarah... God, she tries. She really does. We've been married twenty-two years this October, and she still tries to make things nice for me. And I sat there across from her, and she was talking about her sister's kids, and I'm just sitting there, hearing the words but not really taking them in. I just felt this heavy, thick distance between us. I was just watching her talk, wishing I was back upstairs in the dark so I wouldn't have to try anymore. I love her, I do, but being around her, having to pretend I'm present in the evening... it's just exhausting. It takes so much effort to just nod and say "that's nice." 

And as for other people? No. I avoid them. There's this group of guys, other contractors and a couple of plumbers I've known for years. We used to meet up at O'Malley's on Thursday nights for a couple of pints and to shoot some pool. Complain about clients, talk about material costs, you know. I haven't been in... God, it has to be over a year. When my phone buzzes and I see it's Dave or Mike texting to see if I'm coming out, I don't even open the message. I just swipe it away. The thought of sitting in that loud bar, with the neon signs buzzing and everyone laughing and slapping each other on the back... it just feels impossible. I don't have it in me to put on the mask and act like one of the guys. It's easier to just be alone in the shop. Not that being alone feels good, it's just... it's less work. So, no, I wouldn't say I enjoy spending time with anyone. I just kind of tolerate it when I absolutely have to.

I mean, I know I just sat here and told you how pointless everything feels, and how I can't even look at a piece of oak without feeling like I'm carrying a hundred-pound sack of cement on my shoulders. No. I've never sat down and made a plan or thought about, you know, how I would do it. \n\nI guess... I guess it's more like I just wouldn't mind if I didn't wake up. But taking my own life? I couldn't do that to Sarah. My wife, I mean. She's already stressed enough about the bank and the studio, and she's been trying so hard to keep everything afloat while I've been... like this. If I did something like that, she'd be left with the mortgage, the business loans, the half-finished vanity for the Henderson's... all of it. I couldn't leave her with that mess. I just... I just wish I could go to sleep and not have to deal with it anymore, you know? But I wouldn't actually do anything to make that happen. I just keep slogging through, even though I don't see the point.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this way, like everything is pointless and you're carrying a heavy weight?\n\nPatient: How long? Gosh... it's been a while. I can actually pinpoint it, really. It all started going downhill right around the time I took on the mortgage for the studio. We were renting a smaller place before that, just a little two-bay garage setup, and it was tight, but it was manageable. Then this bigger property came up, and I thought, you know, this is it. This is how I expand. But the second I signed those papers... man, that's when this whole heavy feeling really set in. \n\nThat was a little over two years ago. I remember it was right before the holidays, so it's been about two years and two months now. Two years and two months of waking up every single day feeling like I'm just drowning in it. I remember sitting in that bank office, looking at the loan officer—this kid in a cheap suit who probably didn't know the first thing about building anything with his own two hands—and just signing my life away. I thought owning the building would give me this sense of freedom, like I had finally made it after twenty-some years in the trade. But almost from the very next morning, it was just... pressure. \n\nEvery single board I cut had to pay for that building. Every hour I spent sweeping the floors felt like I was bleeding money. And the weight of it just piled up, day after day, month after month. Sarah kept telling me to give it time, that we'd grow into the space, but it never felt like growing. It just felt like I was being buried alive under all that debt and expectation. So yeah... about two years and two months of just carrying this around, feeling like none of it even matters anymore. I just can't shake it.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever heard voices or seen things that other people couldn't hear or see?\n\nPatient: Voices? Or seeing things? No. No, nothing like that. Especially late at night when Sarah's gone to bed and I'm just sitting out there on my stool, staring at that damn oak vanity. I just feel completely wiped out. \n\nI remember a time, maybe five or six years ago, when I could work a twelve-hour day, frame out a whole kitchen, install the uppers, and still have enough energy to come home and grill steaks in the backyard with Sarah. This is just a heavy, dragging exhaustion that never goes away, no matter how much I sleep or how much coffee I drink. I just stand there in the shop, staring at the tools, feeling like I'm moving through molasses. So, no, I definitely don't have the energy to do what I need to do. Focus? Yeah. Yeah, it's... it's a real problem. It's like my brain is just packed full of sawdust, you know? Just thick and slow. 

I used to be sharp. You have to be, in my line of work. When you're dealing with expensive hardwoods—like this figured maple I had for a custom built-in last year, stuff was eighty dollars a board foot—you measure twice, cut once, right? That's the old saying. But now? I measure three, four, five times, and I still just stand there staring at the tape measure, trying to remember what the little hash marks mean. It's like the numbers just slide right off my brain. Just the other day, I was trying to figure out the angles for some crown molding on a cabinet job. It's a compound miter, which used to be second nature to me. I've done it a thousand times. But I stood there at the saw for twenty minutes, just looking at the protractor, my mind completely blank. I ended up cutting it wrong anyway and wasting a twelve-foot piece of prime stock. 

And making a decision? Forget about it. It's not even just the big things, like whether to take on a new client or what kind of finish to use on a tabletop. It's the stupid, everyday stuff. I went to the hardware store on Tuesday to get screws. Just regular, two-inch construction screws. There were three different brands on the shelf. The yellow box, the green box, the blue box. Same price, same basic screw. I stood in aisle four for... I don't even know how long. Ten minutes? Fifteen? Just staring at them, unable to pick one. My chest started feeling tight, and I just felt so overwhelmed by having to choose a box of screws that I almost walked out without them. I ended up just grabbing the green one because it was closest to my hand, but even then, I worried the whole drive back to the shop if I'd made a mistake. It's ridiculous. I'm a grown man, a carpenter with twenty-five years of experience, and I can't even pick out a box of fasteners without feeling like I'm trying to defuse a bomb. My head just feels so muddy all the time.

Moving slower? Or... no, not really having trouble sitting still, no. I mean, I don't think my body is actually moving any slower when I *do* move. Fidgeting? No. No, like I was just saying a few minutes ago about that brown recliner... I really don't get restless at all. It's actually the exact opposite. 

You know how some guys, when they sit down, they've always got a leg bouncing up and down? Like they're tapping out a drum solo on the floorboards? I had an apprentice like that a couple of years back, a young kid named Tyler. Good kid, hard worker, but he couldn't stand still if his life depended on it. Always spinning a pencil, clicking a utility knife open and closed, tapping his tape measure against his thigh, shifting his weight from his left steel-toe to his right when we were looking over blueprints. Drove me half crazy, to be honest. 

But me? No. I don't do any of that. When I sit down, I am just... planted. My hands, they just sit right there on my lap. These hands have been working wood for twenty-five years, they're beat up, usually covered in calluses and dried wood glue, and they just... stop moving. I don't pick at my cuticles. I don't twiddle my thumbs. I don't shift around trying to get comfortable. Even when I'm standing out in the shop at the main workbench, just staring at a piece of red oak that I'm supposed to be milling down, I'm just rooted to the concrete floor. 

It's like the signal from my brain to my muscles that says, "hey, tap your foot" or "hey, shift your weight," just got completely disconnected somewhere along the line. I just don't have that nervous energy. Any energy, really. So, no, no fidgeting. No restlessness. Just dead still. Like a piece of furniture myself, I guess.

Hobbies? Enjoyable? No. Honestly, no. I mean, it's funny you ask about hobbies, because for a long time, my job was my hobby. Woodworking. Carpentry. That was my whole life, really. I started when I was just a kid in high school, taking shop class with Mr. Henderson. Returning phone calls to clients, trying to explain why a custom cabinet is delayed, or just looking at the invoices piled up on my desk... I can barely do it. I just feel completely wiped out. \n\nI remember a time, maybe five or six years ago, when I could work a twelve-hour day, frame out a whole kitchen, install the uppers, and still have enough energy to come home and grill steaks in the backyard with Sarah. I used to thrive on that kind of momentum. I liked the sweat, the ache in my muscles—it felt earned. But this? This isn't that good, honest kind of tired. This is just a heavy, dragging exhaustion that never goes away, no matter how much I sleep or how much coffee I drink. I just stand there in the shop, staring at the tools, feeling like I'm moving through molasses. So, no, I definitely don't have the energy to do what I need to do. We used to love fishing for bass in the early mornings. But... I spent two weeks dreading it. The packing, the driving, the sun beating down. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Restless? Agitated? No... no, I wouldn't say that at all. Actually, it's pretty much the exact opposite. 

You know, you hear about guys who can't work, and they start pacing the floors, right? Like my buddy Mike. He blew out his knee a few years back—tore his meniscus on a framing job over in Springfield, stepped right in a mud rut while he was carrying a heavy load of two-by-sixes—and he was out of commission for three months. He told me he was crawling out of his skin the whole time. He was taking apart his kitchen appliances, oiling hinges on doors that didn't even squeak, just because he had to be doing *something*. He had all this nervous energy built up and nowhere to put it. 

But me? I don't get that. I don't have any nervous energy. Honestly, I don't have *any* energy. When I'm not working on something—which, like I was just telling you, is pretty much all the time lately—I just sit. I have this old brown corduroy La-Z-Boy recliner in the living room. I bought it at a Sears back in '98, I think. Best chair I've ever owned, even though the footrest lever on the right side sticks a little bit now and you kind of have to kick it to get it to go down. I'll just sit down in that chair, and I won't move for hours. 

I don't tap my foot. I don't wring my hands. I don't feel like I need to get up and pace the hallway. I don't get twitchy or anxious about the fact that I'm not out in the shop. I just... sit there. Sometimes I'll stare at the grain pattern on the hardwood floor—it's red oak, I laid it myself about ten years ago, finished it with three coats of oil-based polyurethane so it would really hold up to heavy boots—and I'll just look at it without even really seeing it. The clock will just tick by. Two hours, three hours. And I don't feel the urge to move at all. 

So, no, there's no restlessness. There's no agitation. It's more like... I don't know, like I'm an eighty-pound bag of Quikrete that got left out in the rain. Just heavy, solid, and stuck in one spot. I could sit there all day and not feel a single itch to get up and do anything.

And the whole time we were actually out there on the water, I was just staring at the ripples, waiting for it to be over so I could go back home and sit in my chair. There's just no spark anymore. I look at my week, or the weekend, or even just dinner tonight, and it's just a long stretch of gray. It's all just things I have to get through, one after the other, until I can finally go back to sleep. So, no. I'm not looking forward to anything. It all just feels like a burden now.\n\nDoctor: Do you still enjoy spending time with your wife and other people?\n\nPatient: Enjoy? I... I don't really know if enjoy is the right word. I don't think I enjoy much of anything, like I was just saying. \n\nWith Sarah... God, she tries. She really does. We've been married twenty-two years this October, and she still tries to make things nice for me. Like, just this past Sunday, she spent all afternoon making a pot roast. The whole house smelled like rosemary and beef stock, the way it used to when we'd have people over back when we first bought the place. She even set the dining room table—the big maple one I turned the legs for on my old Delta lathe, back before I had to sell it—instead of us just eating off our laps in the living room. And I sat there across from her, and she was talking about her sister's kids, and I'm just sitting there, hearing the words but not really taking them in. I just felt this heavy, thick distance between us. I was just watching her talk, wishing I was back upstairs in the dark so I wouldn't have to try anymore. I love her, I do, but being around her, having to pretend I'm present in the evening... it's just exhausting. It takes so much effort to just nod and say \"that's nice.\" \n\nAnd as for other people? No. I avoid them. There's this group of guys, other contractors and a couple of plumbers I've known for years. We used to meet up at O'Malley's on Thursday nights for a couple of pints and to shoot some pool. Complain about clients, talk about material costs, you know. I haven't been in... God, it has to be over a year. When my phone buzzes and I see it's Dave or Mike texting to see if I'm coming out, I don't even open the message. I just swipe it away. The thought of sitting in that loud bar, with the neon signs buzzing and everyone laughing and slapping each other on the back... it just feels impossible. I don't have it in me to put on the mask and act like one of the guys. It's easier to just be alone in the shop. Not that being alone feels good, it's just... it's less work. So, no, I wouldn't say I enjoy spending time with anyone. I just kind of tolerate it when I absolutely have to.\n\nDoctor: Do you find it hard to focus on tasks or make decisions?\n\nPatient: Focus? Yeah. Yeah, it's... it's a real problem. It's like my brain is just packed full of sawdust, you know? Just thick and slow. \n\nI used to be sharp. You have to be, in my line of work. When you're dealing with expensive hardwoods—like this figured maple I had for a custom built-in last year, stuff was eighty dollars a board foot—you measure twice, cut once, right? That's the old saying. But now? I measure three, four, five times, and I still just stand there staring at the tape measure, trying to remember what the little hash marks mean. It's like the numbers just slide right off my brain. Just the other day, I was trying to figure out the angles for some crown molding on a cabinet job. It's a compound miter, which used to be second nature to me. I've done it a thousand times. But I stood there at the saw for twenty minutes, just looking at the protractor, my mind completely blank. I ended up cutting it wrong anyway and wasting a twelve-foot piece of prime stock. \n\nAnd making a decision? Forget about it. It's not even just the big things, like whether to take on a new client or what kind of finish to use on a tabletop. It's the stupid, everyday stuff. I went to the hardware store on Tuesday to get screws. Just regular, two-inch construction screws. There were three different brands on the shelf. The yellow box, the green box, the blue box. Same price, same basic screw. I stood in aisle four for... I don't even know how long. Ten minutes? Fifteen? Just staring at them, unable to pick one. My chest started feeling tight, and I just felt so overwhelmed by having to choose a box of screws that I almost walked out without them. I ended up just grabbing the green one because it was closest to my hand, but even then, I worried the whole drive back to the shop if I'd made a mistake. It's ridiculous. I'm a grown man, a carpenter with twenty-five years of experience, and I can't even pick out a box of fasteners without feeling like I'm trying to defuse a bomb. My head just feels so muddy all the time.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself moving more slowly than you used to, or having trouble sitting still?\n\nPatient: Moving slower? Or... no, not really having trouble sitting still, no. I mean, I don't think my body is actually moving any slower when I *do* move. It's not like my limbs are physically weighed down or I'm walking through mud or anything like that. When I'm out in the shop and I need to walk from the table saw over to the miter station—which is a good twenty feet, I set the shop up that way on purpose so I'd have plenty of clearance for swinging long boards around—my legs work just fine. I walk at a normal pace. I reach for my clamps or my orbital sander at the same speed I always have. It's just... getting the drive to actually initiate the movement, you know? But the physical movement itself isn't slow. I haven't noticed anything like that.\n\nAnd as for sitting still... God, sitting still is about all I do anymore. I definitely don't have any trouble with that. I'm not jittery or restless, I'm not pacing the floors or tapping my foot or anything. I actually have this old brown leather recliner in the corner of the living room. Sarah bought it for me, gosh, maybe five or six years ago from that big furniture warehouse out on Route 9, the one that used to be a roller rink back in the eighties. It's one of those big overstuffed ones. Anyway, I can sit in that chair for hours. Literally hours, without moving a single muscle. \n\nI just sink into the leather and stare straight ahead at the wall. Sometimes the TV is on, playing some rerun I don't care about, but half the time it's just a blank black screen, and I'll just sit there, perfectly still. Sarah will come in from the kitchen with a glass of water or something to check on me, and she'll ask if I'm asleep because I haven't even shifted my weight or moved my arms since she last looked in on me forty-five minutes ago. I just feel so completely drained. So, no, no trouble sitting still at all. If anything, I'm too good at sitting still. I just don't have any urge to get up and move around once I'm down.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're resting or sleeping more than usual?\n\nPatient: Sleeping more? No... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I guess you might think so, right? Given what I just told you about sitting in that brown leather recliner all evening. You'd look at that and think, \"Oh, he's resting.\" But it's not resting. It's just... being stationary. There's a big difference, you know? When you really rest, your body is recovering. Like, back in the day, after a twelve-hour shift pouring concrete or framing out a roof in the July heat, you'd sit down on the porch with a cold beer and you could literally feel your muscles thanking you. Your bones would settle. That's rest. What I do now, just sinking into that chair and staring at the drywall... it doesn't recharge anything. I get up feeling just as heavy as when I sat down.\n\nAnd as for actual sleep in a bed? No, I'm definitely not sleeping more than I used to. I've had the exact same schedule since I was nineteen years old and started my carpenter's apprenticeship with old man Henderson. He was a hardass, excuse my language, but he'd fire you on the spot if you weren't on the job site with your tool belt buckled by 6:00 AM sharp. So my body is just hardwired for it. My alarm still goes off at 5:30 every single morning. It's this old Sony radio alarm clock I've had since the late nineties, the kind with the big red digital numbers that are almost too bright in the dark. It goes off, and I'm out of bed. Even now, when half the time I don't even have a client lined up for the day, or I just plan to shuffle out to my own shop in the garage to look at scrap wood, I still get up at 5:30. \n\nI don't take naps, either. I've never been a nap guy. Sarah, she can lie down on the sofa on a Sunday afternoon at two o'clock and be dead to the world for an hour, but if I try to lie down in the middle of the day, my eyes just stay wide open. We have a really nice mattress, too. It's a big King-size Serta pillow-top we bought back in, gosh, 2015, I think? I remember because my lower back was giving me absolute hell from doing all the custom cabinetry for that big subdivision over in Westlake. It cost a small fortune, but it's comfortable as anything. Still, I don't spend any extra time in it. I go upstairs at 10:30, watch the local news for maybe ten minutes, turn off the lamp, and I'm up at 5:30. Every day. So, no, the hours haven't changed at all. I'm not sleeping the days away. I'm just... awake. Always spinning a pencil, clicking a utility knife open and closed, tapping his tape measure against his thigh, shifting his weight from his left steel-toe to his right when we were looking over blueprints. These hands have been working wood for twenty-five years, they're beat up, usually covered in calluses and dried wood glue, and they just... stop moving. I don't pick at my cuticles. I don't twiddle my thumbs. I don't shift around trying to get comfortable. It's the engine turning over. Once I have to react to something, or once I'm already moving, the speed is completely normal. So, no, to answer your question, my movements and reactions haven't slowed down at all.\n\nDoctor: Are there any hobbies or activities that you still find interesting or enjoyable?\n\nPatient: Hobbies? Enjoyable? No. Honestly, no. I mean, it's funny you ask about hobbies, because for a long time, my job was my hobby. Woodworking. Carpentry. That was my whole life, really. I started when I was just a kid in high school, taking shop class with Mr. Henderson. He was this old, gruff guy missing half his left index finger—which, looking back, probably should have been a warning sign, but he taught me how to respect the tools. How to listen to the wood. \n\nFor twenty-five years, that's what I did. The thought of measuring, cutting, sanding... it just feels pointless. It feels like climbing a mountain just to realize there's nothing at the top. I don't get any joy out of it. I used to like grilling out on the back deck, making burgers or a good ribeye, but now I just eat whatever's easiest. Usually cold cereal or a sandwich. There's just no spark left for anything. No interest. No enjoyment. It's all just gone completely flat.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're restless or agitated when you're not working on something?\n\nPatient: Restless? Agitated? No... no, I wouldn't say that at all. Actually, it's pretty much the exact opposite. \n\nYou know, you hear about guys who can't work, and they start pacing the floors, right? Like my buddy Mike. He blew out his knee a few years back—tore his meniscus on a framing job over in Springfield, stepped right in a mud rut while he was carrying a heavy load of two-by-sixes—and he was out of commission for three months. He told me he was crawling out of his skin the whole time. He was taking apart his kitchen appliances, oiling hinges on doors that didn't even squeak, just because he had to be doing *something*. He had all this nervous energy built up and nowhere to put it. \n\nBut me? I don't get that. I don't have any nervous energy. Honestly, I don't have *any* energy. I don't get twitchy or anxious about the fact that I'm not out in the shop. I just... sit there. Worthlessness. Yeah. Yeah, I’d say that’s a pretty good word for it. It’s... it’s heavy. 

You know, I was telling you about my shop and my tools, and how I’ve had my own studio for a while now. When you run your own shop, your name is on every single piece that goes out the door. You’re not just a guy on an assembly line hiding behind a corporate logo. It's just you.

So, if I’m out there—on the rare occasion I actually try to force myself to do something lately—and I make a mistake... it just destroys me. Like, let’s say I’m cutting a mortise and tenon joint, or maybe hand-cutting some half-blind dovetails for a drawer front. That takes precision. You’re working with fractions of a millimeter, marking it out with a marking knife, not a pencil, so you get a perfect edge. If I put those two pieces of wood together and the joint doesn't line up perfect... if there’s even a hairline gap where light shines through... I don't just look at it and think, "Oh well, I made a mistake, let me grab another piece of stock and try again." 

Or, you know, on the business side of things. Putting together bids for clients. You have to calculate board footage, figure out the waste factor, factor in your time, the cost of the finishes, all of it. It’s a lot of math and planning. And if I miss a bid deadline because I just couldn't get my act together to finish the paperwork, or because I was just sitting in that recliner staring at the floor... 

When stuff like that happens, my brain just goes to the darkest place. I don't just think it's a simple error. I start thinking I'm a completely lousy carpenter. Just a total hack who's been faking it for twenty-five years. I'll stand there looking at a messed-up cut or a missed email, and I'll start telling myself that I had absolutely no business ever trying to run my own studio. I think, who do I think I am? I should have just stayed a grunt on a rough framing crew, banging two-by-fours together for some big contractor who actually knows what they're doing. It just spirals out of control from one little mistake into this huge... this huge conviction that I'm completely useless at the only thing I've ever known how to do. So yeah, I definitely feel that way. A lot.

I don't see how anything is ever going to get better.\n\nDoctor: Do you still find pleasure in the things you used to enjoy, like building custom cabinets?\n\nPatient: Pleasure? I... I don't even know if I'd use that word, or if I even remember what that really feels like, to be honest with you. It's hard to say. I mean, I guess I used to. I used to love the smell of the sawdust, you know? When you first cut into a fresh piece of cherry wood or mahogany... there's this sweet, almost earthy smell that just fills the whole shop. It gets in your clothes, your hair. My wife used to say I smelled like a forest when I came in for dinner. And I used to spend hours, just hours, sanding down the edges of a cabinet door, making sure the joints were perfectly flush. I only do dovetail joints, none of that cheap factory-made stuff with the staples and the glue. I'd run my bare hand over the final finish and just feel... proud, I guess? \n\nBut now... It's been taking up space for three weeks. The client keeps calling, leaving voicemails, and my wife keeps telling me I need to go out there and finish it because the bank is breathing down our necks, and I know she's right. I know it. But I just... I go out there, I pick up the orbital sander, and I just stare at it. I don't feel any spark, I don't feel any pride. I'm not sure I feel anything except just this heavy, exhausting weight I told you about. So, pleasure? I really couldn't tell you. I haven't noticed feeling good about a piece of furniture in... gosh, years, maybe. It's just a block of dead wood to me now. Just another thing I have to do and can't bring myself to care about.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever thought about ending your life?\n\nPatient: End my life? No... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I know I just sat here and told you how pointless everything feels, and how I can't even look at a piece of oak without feeling like I'm carrying a hundred-pound sack of cement on my shoulders. And it's true, it really is. I wake up, and the thought of just... existing... it's exhausting. But actually doing something to end it? No. I've never sat down and made a plan or thought about, you know, how I would do it. \n\nI guess... I guess it's more like I just wouldn't mind if I didn't wake up. Like, if my heart just stopped in my sleep, or if I got into a wreck on the way to the lumber yard and that was just it. That would be okay with me. It would just be quiet, finally. But taking my own life? I couldn't do that to Sarah. My wife, I mean. She's already stressed enough about the bank and the studio, and she's been trying so hard to keep everything afloat while I've been... like this. If I did something like that, she'd be left with the mortgage, the business loans, the half-finished vanity for the Henderson's... all of it. I couldn't leave her with that mess. I just... I just wish I could go to sleep and not have to deal with it anymore, you know? But I wouldn't actually do anything to make that happen. I just keep slogging through, even though I don't see the point.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this way, like everything is pointless and you're carrying a heavy weight?\n\nPatient: How long? Gosh... it's been a while. I can actually pinpoint it, really. It all started going downhill right around the time I took on the mortgage for the studio. We were renting a smaller place before that, just a little two-bay garage setup, and it was tight, but it was manageable. Then this bigger property came up, and I thought, you know, this is it. This is how I expand. But the second I signed those papers... man, that's when this whole heavy feeling really set in. \n\nThat was a little over two years ago. I remember it was right before the holidays, so it's been about two years and two months now. Two years and two months of waking up every single day feeling like I'm just drowning in it. I remember sitting in that bank office, looking at the loan officer—this kid in a cheap suit who probably didn't know the first thing about building anything with his own two hands—and just signing my life away. I thought owning the building would give me this sense of freedom, like I had finally made it after twenty-some years in the trade. But almost from the very next morning, it was just... pressure. \n\nEvery single board I cut had to pay for that building. Every hour I spent sweeping the floors felt like I was bleeding money. And the weight of it just piled up, day after day, month after month. Sarah kept telling me to give it time, that we'd grow into the space, but it never felt like growing. It just felt like I was being buried alive under all that debt and expectation. So yeah... about two years and two months of just carrying this around, feeling like none of it even matters anymore. I just can't shake it.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever heard voices or seen things that other people couldn't hear or see?\n\nPatient: Voices? Or seeing things? No. No, nothing like that. I mean, I know my mind's a mess right now, and I feel like I'm dragging myself through mud every single day, but I'm not... I'm not losing my grip on reality, if that's what you mean. \n\nI mean, the shop gets quiet, you know? Really quiet. Especially late at night when Sarah's gone to bed and I'm just sitting out there on my stool, staring at that damn oak vanity. Sometimes the wind howls around the corrugated metal siding of the new building—it's got this weird rattle to it that the old place never had. The old place was cinderblock, solid, you know? But this new place, it groans and creaks when the temperature drops. And sometimes, I swear, the dust collection system makes this high-pitched whine even when it's turned off, just from the draft pulling through the vents. But that's just the building. That's just air and metal. It's not voices. \n\nI don't hear people talking to me when nobody's there. I don't see shadows moving around or anything crazy like that. It's just... it's just me. Just me and the quiet, and that heavy feeling. Honestly, sometimes I think hearing a voice might actually be a relief, just to break up the silence and the constant loop in my head about the mortgage and the unfinished work and how tired I am. But no, it's just my own thoughts. Just my own miserable thoughts going round and round. No ghosts, no voices, no hallucinations. Just me in an empty shop that I can't afford, staring at wood I don't want to cut.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight recently?\n\nPatient: Weight? No, I... I wear these heavy Carhartt work pants—the double-front ones, you know, because I'm always kneeling on the concrete floor—and they've got a pretty rigid waistband. If I was gaining or losing a lot, I'd definitely feel it there first. But I'm still using the same notch on my leather belt. It's this thick belt I made myself, actually, out of some scrap saddle leather I got from a buddy of mine a few years back. It's got this nice patina on it now, and the buckle hole I always use is worn right in. I haven't had to move it tighter or looser. \n\nI guess my appetite hasn't really changed much either. Sarah still packs my lunch every morning—usually a turkey sandwich on wheat, an apple, and a thermos of black coffee. I eat it out of habit more than anything else. I don't really taste it anymore, to be honest. It's just fuel to keep me standing up at the workbench. And dinners... well, she cooks, and I eat what's in front of me. Sometimes it's meatloaf, sometimes it's just soup if she's had a long day at the studio too. I just kind of chew and swallow while I stare at the wall, thinking about the bills. So, yeah, I'm pretty sure I'm sitting right around the same 185 pounds I've been since I was thirty. The scale in the bathroom is broken anyway—the little dial gets stuck around 150—so I couldn't give you an exact number, but just going by how I feel in my clothes, it hasn't changed. Nothing really changes. Just the same heavy feeling every day.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having trouble sleeping?\n\nPatient: Sleep? No... no, sleep isn't really an issue for me. I don't have any trouble with that. \n\nI mean, by the time I finally drag myself in from the shop, I'm just dead on my feet. I usually lock up the bays around nine, maybe nine-thirty. Sarah always leaves the porch light on for me—just that yellow bug light, you know?—and I come in through the mudroom. I use that orange pumice soap, the heavy-duty stuff, because otherwise the stain just sets right into the calluses on my palms. But anyway, by the time I actually make it upstairs and drop into bed... I'm out before my head even hits the pillow. \n\nWe have this older mattress, a really firm one, because my lower back gets pretty stiff from wrestling with heavy sheet goods all day. I actually built the bed frame myself a few years ago. Solid cherry wood, all mortise and tenon joints, not a single metal screw or fastener in the whole thing. It took me about three months of weekends back when I actually used to enjoy building things for our own house. But yeah, I just sink into that mattress and I'm gone. I sleep right through the night, a solid seven or eight hours, usually. \n\nIt's not the sleeping that's the problem. It's... it's the waking up. That alarm goes off at 5:30 every morning—it's this old digital Sony clock radio Sarah's had since we were in our twenties, got this awful, jarring buzz to it—and the second I hear it, before I even open my eyes, that heavy feeling is just right there waiting for me. It's like the mortgage and the shop and that whole pointless feeling just drop right back onto my chest the exact second I wake up. I just lie there staring at the ceiling, dreading having to put my boots back on. But the actual sleeping part? No. I sleep like a rock. Honestly, sometimes I wish I could just keep sleeping, just so I wouldn't have to get up and face that empty building again. But no, I don't have trouble falling asleep or anything.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you have enough energy to do the things you need to do?\n\nPatient: Energy? No. God, no. I don't have energy for anything anymore. It's... it's like my tank is just permanently on empty, you know? \n\nI mean, I just told you I sleep like a rock, right? Seven, eight hours of solid sleep on that firm cherry wood bed I built. You'd think I'd wake up refreshed, ready to tackle the day, but I don't. I wake up and I'm already exhausted. It's a bone-deep kind of tired. By midmorning, usually around 10 or 10:30, after I've had my coffee and maybe run the table saw for a bit... my arms feel like lead. They feel like I've been hauling wet pressure-treated lumber all day long, just heavy and useless. And that's just from doing basic stuff. \n\nEven just pushing through the normal routine—measuring out cuts, standing at the chop saw, trying to focus on the grain of the wood so I don't mess up a piece of expensive white oak—it takes everything I have. And it's not just the physical work, either. It's the mental stuff. Returning phone calls to clients, trying to explain why a custom cabinet is delayed, or just looking at the invoices piled up on my desk... I can barely do it. I just feel completely wiped out. \n\nI remember a time, maybe five or six years ago, when I could work a twelve-hour day, frame out a whole kitchen, install the uppers, and still have enough energy to come home and grill steaks in the backyard with Sarah. I used to thrive on that kind of momentum. I liked the sweat, the ache in my muscles—it felt earned. But this? This isn't that good, honest kind of tired. This is just a heavy, dragging exhaustion that never goes away, no matter how much I sleep or how much coffee I drink. I just stand there in the shop, staring at the tools, feeling like I'm moving through molasses. So, no, I definitely don't have the energy to do what I need to do. I barely have the energy to stand upright most days.\n\nDoctor: Are there any activities that you still look forward to doing?\n\nPatient: Look forward to? No. No, not really. I... I can't really think of a single thing. \n\nIt's funny, because I used to have a lot of things. I used to love going down to MacGregor's—that's the specialty lumber yard about forty minutes from here, out past the county line. I used to wake up early on a Saturday, grab a coffee, and just go walk the aisles. The smell of the rough-sawn walnut, the kiln-dried cherry... I could spend hours just looking at the grain patterns on the live-edge slabs, imagining what I could build. A dining table, a custom credenza. I'd run my hands over the rough edges and just feel this... excitement, you know? Like potential. I'd look forward to that trip all week. \n\nBut now? Now if I have to go to MacGregor's to pick up stock for a job, it's just a chore. It's just heavy lifting and traffic and spending money I barely have. I walk past those same stacks of beautiful walnut and I don't feel a damn thing. Just... nothing. I just look at it and think about the weight of having to haul it into the truck, mill it down, joint it, plane it, sand it until my shoulders scream. \n\nSarah even tried to get me to go to the lake last month, thought maybe getting the old aluminum boat out would help. We used to love fishing for bass in the early mornings. But... I spent two weeks dreading it. The packing, the driving, the sun beating down. And the whole time we were actually out there on the water, I was just staring at the ripples, waiting for it to be over so I could go back home and sit in my chair. There's just no spark anymore. I look at my week, or the weekend, or even just dinner tonight, and it's just a long stretch of gray. It's all just things I have to get through, one after the other, until I can finally go back to sleep. So, no. I'm not looking forward to anything. It all just feels like a burden now.\n\nDoctor: Do you still enjoy spending time with your wife and other people?\n\nPatient: Enjoy? I... I don't really know if enjoy is the right word. I don't think I enjoy much of anything, like I was just saying. \n\nWith Sarah... God, she tries. She really does. We've been married twenty-two years this October, and she still tries to make things nice for me. Like, just this past Sunday, she spent all afternoon making a pot roast. The whole house smelled like rosemary and beef stock, the way it used to when we'd have people over back when we first bought the place. She even set the dining room table—the big maple one I turned the legs for on my old Delta lathe, back before I had to sell it—instead of us just eating off our laps in the living room. I just felt this heavy, thick distance between us. I was just watching her talk, wishing I was back upstairs in the dark so I wouldn't have to try anymore. No. I avoid them. There's this group of guys, other contractors and a couple of plumbers I've known for years. We used to meet up at O'Malley's on Thursday nights for a couple of pints and to shoot some pool. Complain about clients, talk about material costs, you know. I haven't been in... God, it has to be over a year. When my phone buzzes and I see it's Dave or Mike texting to see if I'm coming out, I don't even open the message. I just swipe it away. The thought of sitting in that loud bar, with the neon signs buzzing and everyone laughing and slapping each other on the back... it just feels impossible. So, no, I wouldn't say I enjoy spending time with anyone. I just kind of tolerate it when I absolutely have to.\n\nDoctor: Do you find it hard to focus on tasks or make decisions?\n\nPatient: Focus? When you're dealing with expensive hardwoods—like this figured maple I had for a custom built-in last year, stuff was eighty dollars a board foot—you measure twice, cut once, right? It's like the numbers just slide right off my brain. Just the other day, I was trying to figure out the angles for some crown molding on a cabinet job. It's a compound miter, which used to be second nature to me. I've done it a thousand times. But I stood there at the saw for twenty minutes, just looking at the protractor, my mind completely blank. I ended up cutting it wrong anyway and wasting a twelve-foot piece of prime stock. \n\nAnd making a decision? Forget about it. It's not even just the big things, like whether to take on a new client or what kind of finish to use on a tabletop. It's the stupid, everyday stuff. I went to the hardware store on Tuesday to get screws. Just regular, two-inch construction screws. There were three different brands on the shelf. The yellow box, the green box, the blue box. My head just feels so muddy all the time.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself moving more slowly than you used to, or having trouble sitting still?\n\nPatient: Moving slower? Or... no, not really having trouble sitting still, no. I mean, I don't think my body is actually moving any slower when I *do* move. I've had the exact same schedule since I was nineteen years old and started my carpenter's apprenticeship with old man Henderson. He was a hardass, excuse my language, but he'd fire you on the spot if you weren't on the job site with your tool belt buckled by 6:00 AM sharp. So my body is just hardwired for it. My alarm still goes off at 5:30 every single morning. I've never been a nap guy. Always spinning a pencil, clicking a utility knife open and closed, tapping his tape measure against his thigh, shifting his weight from his left steel-toe to his right when we were looking over blueprints. Getting the spark to actually stand up and pick up the wood, you know? But the actual walking, the lifting, the reaching? No, I haven't noticed any kind of slow-down with my muscles at all. I really don't think so. I mean, we just talked about the physical moving part, right? My actual movements haven't slowed down. And as for my reactions? No, those are exactly the same too. I haven't lost a step there. \n\nJust... I guess it was last Tuesday? I always change the oil every three thousand miles on the dot, check the fluids, all that stuff. Big buck, right in front of my bumper. \n\nI slammed on the brakes, swerved just a hair to the right, and missed him by absolute inches. My foot hit that brake pedal before my brain even fully registered what I was looking at. I started when I was just a kid in high school, taking shop class with Mr. Henderson. He was this old, gruff guy missing half his left index finger—which, looking back, probably should have been a warning sign, but he taught me how to respect the tools. No interest. No enjoyment. It's all just gone completely flat.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're restless or agitated when you're not working on something?\n\nPatient: Restless? Agitated? No... no, I wouldn't say that at all. Actually, it's pretty much the exact opposite. \n\nYou know, you hear about guys who can't work, and they start pacing the floors, right? Like my buddy Mike. He blew out his knee a few years back—tore his meniscus on a framing job over in Springfield, stepped right in a mud rut while he was carrying a heavy load of two-by-sixes—and he was out of commission for three months. He told me he was crawling out of his skin the whole time. He was taking apart his kitchen appliances, oiling hinges on doors that didn't even squeak, just because he had to be doing *something*. He had all this nervous energy built up and nowhere to put it. \n\nBut me? I don't get that. I don't have any nervous energy. Honestly, I don't have *any* energy. When I'm not working on something—which, like I was just telling you, is pretty much all the time lately—I just sit. I have this old brown corduroy La-Z-Boy recliner in the living room. I bought it at a Sears back in '98, I think. Best chair I've ever owned, even though the footrest lever on the right side sticks a little bit now and you kind of have to kick it to get it to go down. I'll just sit down in that chair, and I won't move for hours. \n\nI don't tap my foot. I don't wring my hands. I don't feel like I need to get up and pace the hallway. I don't get twitchy or anxious about the fact that I'm not out in the shop. I just... sit there. Sometimes I'll stare at the grain pattern on the hardwood floor—it's red oak, I laid it myself about ten years ago, finished it with three coats of oil-based polyurethane so it would really hold up to heavy boots—and I'll just look at it without even really seeing it. The clock will just tick by. Two hours, three hours. And I don't feel the urge to move at all. \n\nSo, no, there's no restlessness. There's no agitation. It's more like... I don't know, like I'm an eighty-pound bag of Quikrete that got left out in the rain. Just heavy, solid, and stuck in one spot. I could sit there all day and not feel a single itch to get up and do anything.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any feelings of worthlessness?\n\nPatient: Worthlessness. Yeah. Yeah, I’d say that’s a pretty good word for it. It’s... it’s heavy. \n\nYou know, I was telling you about my shop and my tools, and how I’ve had my own studio for a while now. When you run your own shop, your name is on every single piece that goes out the door. You’re not just a guy on an assembly line hiding behind a corporate logo. It's just you.\n\nSo, if I’m out there—on the rare occasion I actually try to force myself to do something lately—and I make a mistake... it just destroys me. Like, let’s say I’m cutting a mortise and tenon joint, or maybe hand-cutting some half-blind dovetails for a drawer front. That takes precision. You’re working with fractions of a millimeter, marking it out with a marking knife, not a pencil, so you get a perfect edge. If I put those two pieces of wood together and the joint doesn't line up perfect... if there’s even a hairline gap where light shines through... I don't just look at it and think, \"Oh well, I made a mistake, let me grab another piece of stock and try again.\" \n\nOr, you know, on the business side of things. Putting together bids for clients. You have to calculate board footage, figure out the waste factor, factor in your time, the cost of the finishes, all of it. It’s a lot of math and planning. And if I miss a bid deadline because I just couldn't get my act together to finish the paperwork, or because I was just sitting in that recliner staring at the floor... \n\nWhen stuff like that happens, my brain just goes to the darkest place. I don't just think it's a simple error. I start thinking I'm a completely lousy carpenter. Just a total hack who's been faking it for twenty-five years. I'll stand there looking at a messed-up cut or a missed email, and I'll start telling myself that I had absolutely no business ever trying to run my own studio. I think, who do I think I am? I should have just stayed a grunt on a rough framing crew, banging two-by-fours together for some big contractor who actually knows what they're doing. It just spirals out of control from one little mistake into this huge... this huge conviction that I'm completely useless at the only thing I've ever known how to do. So yeah, I definitely feel that way. A lot.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any thoughts of self-harm or suicide in the past two years?\n\nPatient: Self-harm? Suicide? No... no, I haven't. I haven't had any thoughts like that. \n\nI mean, it’s a fair question, I guess, especially considering my line of work. I've got a shop absolutely full of things that could do serious damage if you wanted them to. I've got a 3-horsepower Delta Unisaw sitting right in the middle of the floor, heavy cast-iron top, spins a 10-inch carbide-tipped blade at about four thousand RPMs. I’ve got pneumatic nail guns, plunge routers, Japanese pull saws that cut on the pull stroke and are sharp enough to slice right through bone if you aren't paying attention. You kind of have to respect the danger when you're a carpenter. A dull tool is a dangerous tool, that's what we were always taught. So everything I own is kept razor sharp. \n\nBut... even with all that stuff right there, just sitting on my workbench or hanging on the pegboard... I never look at any of it and think about using it on myself. It just doesn't cross my mind. Not once in the last couple of years, not ever, really. \n\nI think... well, like I was telling you before about sitting in that brown corduroy recliner. I just feel so heavy. So flat. To actually want to hurt yourself, or to make a plan to end your life... I feel like that takes a certain kind of energy. Like you have to be actively desperate, you know? Like a guy trying to break a window to get out of a burning house. But I don't feel like I'm in a burning house. I just feel like I'm sitting in a house where all the lights burned out a long time ago, and I just don't have the energy to get up and change the bulbs. \n\nSo, no. I don't want to die. I really don't. I just... I don't get any joy out of being awake, either. But as far as actually doing something permanent, or hurting myself? No. I wouldn't do that. I just sit there. That's about all I do."
